risks: Minimal for patients: the flag runs in silent mode and no clinical action depends on it; reviewers read messages that are already handled in the usual way.
consent: Individual consent is impracticable for thousands of sampled messages; a waiver of consent is requested, with notices on the portal explaining the study and an opt-out.
data: Message text from clinics A and B is extracted by the informatics nurse under privacy approval PRV-2026-221, pseudonymised, and reviewed on the organisation's secure system; clinic C's messages are not extracted while it is paused.
equity: PROGRESS-Plus: older patients, carers and people writing in languages other than English are at most risk of missed urgent messages. With clinic C paused, messages in other languages are few, so the study cannot yet show whether the flag is safe for them; the report says so, and the flag is not recommended for switch-on for those messages until clinic C's data are added.
effectiveness: The flag is recommended only if sensitivity is acceptable overall and in each subgroup that can be estimated.
efficiency: Reviewer time within the quality budget.
costs: Reviewer and informatics nurse time within the 12,000 quality budget.
grants: A digital health equity grant could fund adding clinic C and interpreters for rating.
partnerships: Clinic directors, the patient advisory group, a community organisation serving patients who write in other languages, and the vendor.
rebPath: Research ethics review of secondary use of message text with a consent waiver under TCPS 2, alongside privacy approval PRV-2026-221, for clinics A and B; an amendment adds clinic C when it resumes.
limitations: Two clinics; few messages in other languages; imperfect reference standard.
summary: Consent waiver and privacy approval for two clinics; the equity gap from clinic C's pause is stated.
